case_studies.title: Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation (ROGUE-AI)
case_studies.abstract: Agents based on large language models (LLMs) can now delete files and send payments on behalf of their users. News media reports routinely describe failures of these agents (e.g., Replit's coding agent deleting a production database), but a report often only says what went wrong and rarely (in)validates the incident or finds its root cause. Incident catalogs collect these reports, and benchmarks record whether agents fail, but neither replicates an incident nor tests the cause its report might identify. In this paper, we present ROGUE-AI (Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation), a multi-agent framework that closes the above gap and rebuilds each reported incident offline together with a matched control that lacks only the blamed cause, and runs agents on both. Our results suggest that ROGUE-AI is able to reproduce the reported harm in 89% of its 108 attempted replications. Agents built on five current GPT, Claude, Gemini and DeepSeek models made the reported mistake in 18% to 33% of runs, against at most 1% without the blamed cause. Of the 72 incidents with real-world harm, 62 had no underlying attacker, and in these, agents did what their task asked for but missed an ordinary hazard, such as a database shared with the live site. Replications without an attacker caused more harm than replications of prompt injection for all five models. Defenses against prompt injection look for injected instructions, but these replications contain none. Further, a warning after each tool output that names the hazard and its consequence lowered harm for all five models, whereas a note of the same length that does not mention the hazard left most of the harm in place. Built from real incidents, the ROGUE-AI replications form a reusable audit framework that vendors can rerun before each new release.
case_studies.summary: ROGUE‑AI builds a test framework that re‑creates real incidents involving LLM agents, such as accidental file deletion or payment fraud, and shows that the agents reproduce the harm 89% of the time. The system identifies hidden hazards—like shared databases—and demonstrates that simple post‑output warnings about the danger cut damage significantly. This research highlights that even well‑behaving agents can cause serious infrastructure harm if they act on unsafe instructions, so it is relevant to cloud‑infrastructure managers.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure that uses LLM‑based agents, step 1: replicate any past incidents with ROGUE‑AI or a similar tool to see if your agents can reproduce the harm. Step 2: identify shared resources (e.g., databases, file shares) that the agents might access. Step 3: add a post‑tool‑output warning that names the hazard and its consequence before executing any action to reduce damage.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a practical, testable framework (ROGUE-AI) that allows IT engineers to reproduce agentic security incidents and validate safeguards. It is built, contains code, and can be deployed immediately. The framework can be marketed as an audit or security testing service for SaaS and cloud environments, directly benefiting IT infrastructure teams.

case_studies.title: HiSA: Sparsifying the Hidden Dimension of RoPE Attention in LLMs
case_studies.abstract: Attention in large language models (LLMs) scores every query against every key with a full dot product. We investigate whether this dot product must be computed completely for attention to be effective. We propose Hidden Sparse Attention (HiSA), which keeps the query and key projections intact but only computes a partial dot product, following a static, parameter-free rule set by the token positions: attention becomes sparse in the hidden (feature) dimension, an axis much less explored than token sparsity, rather than over tokens as in almost all sparse attention methods. Based on the structure of rotary position embeddings (RoPE), we decompose keys and queries into parts which can be omitted when computing attention. By training LLMs from scratch with HiSA, we find that this partial dot product does not hurt but improves performance compared with the complete product while computing only about a third of the query-key products. During inference HiSA improves decoding speed and shrinks memory footprint. We also extend HiSA to FlashAttention-3 kernels for training and inference. Finally, we motivate our approach by showing that dense attention learns to suppress the attention score parts that HiSA drops. Code is available at https://github.com/ambroise-b/hisa.
case_studies.summary: HiSA removes part of the dot product in the feature dimension of RoPE attention, keeping only about a third of the calculations while matching or improving model performance. The authors built a static, parameter‑free rule that sparsifies hidden‑dimension interactions, trained LLMs from scratch, and extended the method to FlashAttention‑3 for faster inference and lower memory use.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, here is what to do: 1) Monitor memory usage of your LLM inference services; 2) Evaluate adopting HiSA to cut per‑token attention cost by ~66%, reducing GPU memory footprint and speeding up response times; 3) Test the HiSA implementation with FlashAttention‑3 in your deployment pipeline to confirm performance gains.
case_studies.relevance_tag: LLM performance optimization, cloud AI deployment
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a concrete optimization (HiSA) that reduces LLM inference time and memory usage by a third, directly benefiting IT engineers managing LLM deployments on cloud infrastructure. Code is released and models trained, indicating practical readiness. The technique can be packaged as a performance‑boosting service or integrated into existing MLOps pipelines, offering clear monetisation potential within a short time frame.

case_studies.title: Validation-driven Deployment of LLM Inference Platforms for Agentic Workloads
case_studies.abstract: Enterprises are moving agentic workloads from closed APIs to their own open-weight model deployments. For this reason, lifecycle-wide validation, from small-scale testing through sizing and pre-production to production, becomes all the more important. Typically, rollouts are evaluated with ad hoc tools whose accuracy is rarely checked. We present an end-to-end evaluation pipeline for agentic LLM serving and empirically ground the design choices that connect its stages. Our experiments show that replaying captured traces reproduces the per-session load of the original agent sessions: at the 95th percentile replay stays within 1.18x of the recorded input tokens while live re-runs reach 4.98x, so a small set of recorded sessions yields a repeatable per-session token load. A code-coverage analysis of vLLM further shows that the evaluated live, replayed, and synthetic workloads are complementary in this configuration: each exercises Python serving paths not reached in the measured runs of the others. In a case study rolling out four large mixture-of-experts (MoE) models on llm-d, experiments show that the target models reached about half the optimal concurrency, and correspondingly about 60% of the throughput, on captured workloads compared with public traces. We open-source the relevant tools and release a trace dataset.
case_studies.summary: The research tackles the problem of reliably validating and scaling large language model (LLM) deployments for agentic workloads. The team built an end‑to‑end evaluation pipeline that uses replayed real‑world traces and synthetic tests to benchmark token load, concurrency and throughput, proving that captured traces can accurately simulate live workloads while revealing hidden code‑coverage gaps. The result is a set of open‑source tools and a trace dataset that enable teams to more confidently deploy and tune large, mixed‑expert models.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM inference infrastructure, use the pipeline: 1) capture real user sessions as traces; 2) replay those traces to generate per‑session token loads that stay within 1.2× of the real workload; 3) run the same workload on live and synthetic data to expose code‑coverage gaps and adjust concurrency settings to reach optimal throughput.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces a practical end-to-end validation pipeline for agentic LLM serving, directly impacting how IT engineers deploy and manage LLM workloads. The authors provide open-source tooling and a trace dataset, indicating a working system rather than a theoretical proposal, which justifies the high AI maturity score. The methods and data are actionable and could be packaged as a service or integrated into existing MLOps workflows, supporting a solid monetisation potential. Overall, the work has significant relevance to infrastructure, automation, and cloud deployment of LLMs.

case_studies.title: Held While Waiting: What LLM Agent Sessions Reserve on Serverless and Agent Runtimes
case_studies.abstract: LLM agents spend nearly all their time waiting for the model. On Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, our agents waited a median of 2.7 seconds for each model reply, then computed for an estimated 5 to 40 milliseconds. AgentCore does not charge for CPU during the wait. But it reserves a separate environment, a virtual machine with its own memory, for every conversation, and keeps it reserved until the conversation is closed. So 1,000 conversations reserve 1,000 environments to do the work of 2 to 15 processor cores. A service runs out of environments long before it runs out of processing power. The shortage has two causes, and each has a fix. An environment stays reserved after its conversation ends: in the customer-service benchmark we ran, a conversation lasts 33 seconds on average, but its environment is held for 15 minutes more unless the client closes it. And an environment serves only one conversation, which is mostly waiting: in our simulation, 64 conversations sharing one environment need 59 times fewer environments, and 99 of every 100 replies are delayed by at most 40 milliseconds. The milliseconds are an estimate because they are hard to measure: a stubbed model, a timer around the model call, and steps run back to back each gave a plausible number that was too low. We show how to avoid all three. Of the two fixes, closing needs only the client. Sharing needs the platform, and of the agent runtimes we surveyed only one allows it, in part. They keep conversations apart because an agent runs tools, and sometimes code, chosen by a model. The open problem is to keep them apart without reserving an environment for each while it waits.
case_studies.summary: The study shows that LLM agents on serverless runtimes keep an entire virtual environment reserved for each conversation, even while waiting for model responses, causing resource waste. The authors built a simulation and benchmarks on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, revealing that 1,000 concurrent chats reserve 1,000 environments, leading to early exhaustion of available environments. They suggest that closing environments promptly and allowing multiple conversations per environment can dramatically improve efficiency.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage a serverless LLM agent platform, first ensure your clients close environments immediately after a conversation ends. Second, modify your runtime to allow a single environment to handle multiple parallel conversations, reducing the number of reserved environments by an order of magnitude. This will free up capacity and lower operational costs.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses a practical infrastructure inefficiency in serverless LLM agent runtimes that directly impacts resource utilization for IT engineers managing cloud services. It presents measurable findings and concrete fixes, indicating that the work is beyond theoretical and has already been validated in experiments, giving it moderate AI maturity. The actionable insights (e.g., environment sharing or explicit closing) provide a clear path for cost optimisation and can be implemented by engineers or offered as a service within 90 days, resulting in a high monetisation potential.

case_studies.title: Aggron: Aggressive Compression of Agentic KV Caches during Head-of-Line Stalls in the Request Queue
case_studies.abstract: LLM agents run long, multi-turn programs whose contexts grow at every step, and serving them is limited by KV cache capacity. To alleviate this limitation, systems use context compression techniques, which typically wait until the KV cache crosses a large threshold and then summarize large spans of history at once, either in the background while the agent progresses or on the critical path. These summarizations can be done using the same model running on the same engine, or using the same or a different model running on extra hardware. When running on the same engine, summarization competes with the requests being served for both compute and memory capacity. To maximize the cost-effectiveness of summarization, this paper presents a new serving system called {\em Aggron}. Aggron summarizes agentic requests at every turn and selectively summarizes only certain parts of the KV cache. As a result, Aggron retains accuracy and keeps summarization requests lightweight. Moreover, Aggron launches summarization requests from a separate {\em Summarization Queue} while the corresponding agentic request whose KV cache we want to compress is stalled in the main request queue due to head-of-line stalls. The Summarization queue utilizes compute and memory capacity left over by the head-of-line stalls in the main queue. Further, to maximize efficiency, the server issues summarizations only when it predicts that they can complete before the corresponding agentic request will finally execute. In our evaluation, we compare Aggron to state-of-the-art asynchronous summarization. At high load, Aggron reduces P99 program latency by $27$--$31\%$, and raises throughput by $1.34$--$1.40\times$.
case_studies.summary: Aggron tackles the problem of limited KV cache capacity for large language model agents by compressing the cache aggressively and selectively during head‑of‑line stalls. It builds a new serving system that queues summarisation tasks separately, using idle compute from stalled requests, and predicts when summarisation can finish before the main request resumes. The result is a 27‑31% drop in 99th‑percentile latency and a 34‑40% boost in throughput at high load.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM agent infrastructure, here is what to do: 1) add a summarisation queue that runs on idle compute from stalled requests; 2) implement selective compression of KV cache sections; 3) predict summarisation completion before the main request resumes and only trigger summarisation then.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a concrete system (Aggron) that directly improves LLM agent serving by reducing latency and increasing throughput, which is highly relevant to IT engineers managing LLM deployments. The solution appears to be a working prototype with published results, indicating a certain level of maturity, though it may not yet be fully productionized. The approach offers actionable insights that could be adopted or sold as a service within 90 days to optimize cloud-based LLM workloads.
